title: I Refused the School-Issued Chromebook for My Middle-Schooler. You Can Too. Heres How
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Cherkin chronicles her decision to opt her daughter out of the school-issued laptop starting in 7th grade after noticing near-daily headaches, negative feelings about school, and unsustainable consumption of pain medication. A former teacher and EdTech advocate, she faced a contradiction: professionally advocating for screen reduction while her child spent hours daily on a school laptop with no parental visibility into sites, apps, or usage. Rather than framing opt-out as tech-opposition, she grounded her approach in tech-intentionality: less is more, later is better, relationships and skills before screens. She built relationships with school leadership first, approaching them as partners rather than adversaries. The process included preparing her daughter for social questions, emailing teachers individually with explanations and offers to support their work, strategizing compromises (home computer access, loaner devices for rare needs), and finding that most teachers responded positively. The result: physical symptoms resolved (the Advil bottle stayed full), her daughter thrived academically without the laptop, and the family continues the practice into high school. Cherkin demonstrates that opting out is feasible when pursued respectfully through relationship-building, honest communication, and willingness to accommodate teachers.
points: Excessive school-issued device use correlates with physical symptoms (headaches) and psychological strain (seeing school as something to endure); removing the device resolved both.
Tech-intentional parenting requires alignment between values and practice; it starts by building relationships and trust with school leadership, not conflict.
Paper-based learning and handwriting practice are viable even in 1:1 device schools; most teachers support thoughtful accommodation when approached respectfully.
Three principles guide tech-intentional childhood: less is more, later is better, relationships and skills before screens.
quotes: But I didn't expect my daughter to start experiencing near-daily headaches. I didn't notice it at first— I just thought she was tired or dehydrated. But then I realized how much pediatric Advil we were going through.

At the same time this was happening, my professional life was all about advocating for reducing, delaying, and limiting screen use in childhood. Yet at school each day, she could theoretically spend hours a day on her laptop at school, and I had no visibility into what she was doing online.

My approach has always been about being tech-intentional. And my definition for this approach is grounded in three simple ideas: Less is more. Later is better. Relationships and skills before screens.
I needed to start by building relationships with the school leadership team. I was polite and appreciative for the work they do and recognized that they were not necessarily the decision-makers.

Because things were planned out, handled in the context of respectful relationships, and my daughter was prepped in advance, our opt-out experience has gone as well as we could have hoped for. Her headaches were gone.” Archived from First Fish Chronicles Substack on May 3, 2026 by Tim.
